chunks: From him, from Muhammad ibn Khalid, from Ibn Bukayr and Al-Nadr, from Al-Qasim ibn Sulayman, all from Ubayd ibn Zur'arah, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him)

Regarding a man who pledged an item with his partner as collateral, and there was no clear evidence between them: The one holding the collateral claimed it was worth one thousand, while the owner of the collateral claimed it was worth one hundred. He (peace be upon him) said: 'The burden of proof is on the one holding the collateral who claims it is worth one thousand; if he has no proof, then the oath is upon the owner of the collateral that it is worth one hundred.'
ai.seo_question: How is the value of disputed collateral determined in Shia Islamic jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This ruling from Imam al-Sadiq (AS) establishes a nuanced evidentiary hierarchy in pledge disputes: the holder bears the burden of proof for any claimed increase in value, while the owner's oath suffices for the original amount if proof is lacking. This principle reflects the Shia jurisprudential emphasis on fairness and the presumption of innocence in financial transactions, ensuring that the party in possession of the asset cannot unilaterally inflate its worth without evidence. It underscores the practical application of 'al-bayyinah ala al-mudda'i' (proof is upon the claimant) within the specific context of rahn (pledge).
